strategy.summary: Reproduce the descending complex sort NaN-ordering bug in numpy's C++ complex_type comparator (numpy_tag.h) by building numpy at the buggy commit b1b77568be65 and running the parametrized test test_sort_descending_complex_lexorder, which must fail on the buggy build and pass on the fixed build. The comparator is C++ and not importable from Python, so the test runs through the compiled numpy extension after an in-tree build.

pinned_because: pytest and hypothesis are documented in README.md with no version constraint, so they are unpinned; the strategy chooses current versions compatible with the Python in use and records that choice here
no numerically relevant dependency constraint is stated in the evidence, so no numpy-side pins beyond the build requirements file at the buggy commit are applied

strategy.success_criterion: On the buggy revision b1b77568be65 the parametrized test_sort_descending_complex_lexorder cases with descending=True fail on the ordering assertion because only-imaginary-NaN entries sort before only-real-NaN entries; on the fixed revision (the PR #31572 change applied, including the rb != rb fallback in complex_type less-than) the same cases pass, so the transition is FAIL to PASS.
strategy.numerical_probe: Not required for grading; the test's isnan-mask ordering check is the probe.

input_output_examples.input: Complex array mixing complex(0, nan) values with complex(nan, 0) values, sorted descending
input_output_examples.buggy_output: Only-imaginary-NaN values appear before only-real-NaN values
input_output_examples.expected_output: Only-real-NaN values appear after only-imaginary-NaN values

risks: The bug is in a C++ header; it only exists in a compiled build of the buggy commit, so the test cannot be run against an installed numpy wheel and requires building from source.
Dtype (complex64 vs complex128) is not stated in the evidence; the test is parametrized over dtype, so both should be run and the failing one identified.
The defect is observed through descending sort only; the stable/descending parametrization must be included in the -k selection, and the test must not be filtered to descending=False.

The comparator behaviour is platform-agnostic in principle, but NaN payload and compiler optimisation (e.g. -ffast-math or aggressive FP contraction) could change whether NaN comparisons are folded; use a standard release build without fast-math.
The PR body is truncated, so the exact expected ordering is taken from the test assertions rather than from the prose.
Build time for numpy from source is long and depends on available cores and a working compiler toolchain; a build failure would prevent any transition check.
The test file path and class name are inferred from the diff context and should be confirmed in the checked-out revision before running.
No sanitiser or specific architecture is evidenced as required, so none is assumed; if the failure only appears on a specific platform, the transition may not reproduce elsewhere.

oracle.reference_source: test_sort_descending_complex_lexorder isnan-mask ordering assertions in numpy/_core/tests/test_multiarray.py
oracle.why: The ordering check is an exact boolean property of NaN positions, not a numerical tolerance.

strategy.fails_on_buggy: The ordering assertion on the descending sort sees only-imaginary-NaN entries ahead of only-real-NaN entries in the buggy comparator's output, violating the expected real-NaN-primary ordering, so the test fails.
strategy.passes_on_fixed: With the rb != rb fallback and direct ra > rb / ra < rb branches in complex_type less-than, only-real-NaN entries sort after only-imaginary-NaN entries in descending order, so the ordering assertion holds and the test passes.
